row.scope_summary: John Gurney's earliest firm New England presence and his arrival window.
row.title: Colonial arrival chronology

row.scope_summary: John Gurney's Braintree residence, the leased Tyng farm (future Adams seat), his Monatiquot freehold, and his standing in the town (c. 1645–1662/3).
row.title: Colonial Braintree community

row.scope_summary: John Gurney's own frontier-plantation proprietary rights, 1659-1663 (Billerica absentee share, Mendon allotment, Quinapaug estate interest); none became residence.
row.title: Colonial frontier rights

row.scope_summary: The material texture of John Gurney's life read from his 1663 estate inventory (SPR Case #338): a modest all-movable estate whose value lay in livestock and farm gear, a sparse household, and the absence of any tailoring tool despite the 'tailor' style in his 1661/2 deed.
row.title: Colonial material life

row.scope_summary: The shape of John Gurney's surviving documentary record — which record classes attest him (civic, land, court, probate) and where the record is silent (vital, church, origin) — as distinct from the substance of any one record and from the deferred identity/origin question.
row.title: Colonial record coverage

row.scope_summary: John Gurney's standing in the Weymouth town community, c. 1638/9-1644: inhabitant land grants, a credit tie to Rev. Thomas Jenner, documented Weymouth associates, and the limits of his militia record. Arrival dating lives in the arrival-chronology unit.
row.title: Colonial Weymouth community

row.scope_summary: Colonial-era same-surname Gurneys outside John's documented family: the Providence, Rhode Island John and Sarah Gurney (1695-1714), an unresolved Suffolk Deeds index entry for a James Gurner, and the resolution of a third apparent Dorchester Gurney thread as the unrelated Gurnell family.
row.title: Family — colonial collaterals

row.scope_summary: John Gurney's children reconstructed as a family group: the five-child roster (Sarah, Mary, Richard, John Jr., Peter) plus the uncertain Isaac, its compiled-genealogy basis, Torrey's family-group cross-check, and the by-elimination Isaac identification. Excludes Mary's marriage (g13-family-wives-marriages), the post-1662 Mendon descendant stream (g13-family-mendon-descendants), Richard's own line (the direct-line G12 subject), and the origin/identity use of the roster.
row.title: Family — the children as a family group

row.scope_summary: John Gurney Jr.'s Mendon household with wife Ruth and their children, his death in the 1675 Mendon massacre and Ruth's remarriage to John Bundy, the two-Johns disambiguation resolving which same-named cousin died there, the separate post-1667 Mendon proprietary lots of John Jr. and his father's widow Grisel, Peter's King Philip's War service and death, and two open leads on a further Taunton-area descendant trail.
row.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

row.scope_summary: John Gurney's two marriages: first wife Mary (English marriage by the mid-1620s, died Braintree 20 Sep 1661) and the widow Grizzell (married Braintree 12 Nov 1661), and the manuscript reading that resolves the misread 'John Cheny' Braintree town-record lines to John Gurney.
row.title: Family — wives and marriages

row.scope_summary: What the identity work adds up to: an identification reached by elimination and circumstantial fit rather than by any document naming John's father. Carries the elimination of Candidate C (Berkhamsted), the last principal alternative without its own unit; the unknown-corridor residual the eliminations do not clear, with the 1662-1666 London Gurney hearth-tax cluster as its density evidence; the open question of whether John emigrated through the Gurdon-Winthrop Court of Wards patronage network; Anderson's "Boston" settlement attribution read as a conflation artifact; and what would move the estimate, including the lag between the fact sheet's published sixty percent and the case file's current ~65%. The parentage argument itself is g13-identity-candidate-b; the probability model is the case file's.
row.title: Identity — assessment

row.scope_summary: Candidate A's Stewkley-to-Aylesbury-to-Walgrave Buckinghamshire/Northamptonshire chain, the wider Bucks Gurney household map, and the 1661 Edlesborough marriage that independently reinforce his elimination as the Massachusetts emigrant.
row.title: Identity — Candidate A: Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire

row.scope_summary: The 1636 Ackworth marriage of John Gurnoe to Mary Burton, the sole other wife-name match in the record sweeps, held at a residual ~3% rather than eliminated outright.
row.title: Identity — Ackworth, Yorkshire

row.scope_summary: The surviving candidate's own parentage argument: John Gurney of Braintree as the son of Francis Gurney, Merchant Taylor of West Barsham, Norwich and London, by his first wife Margaret Rybett. Carries Francis's identity and finances, the 1611 Norwich marriage discovery, Margaret's Rivett kin near East Dereham, the East Dereham child cluster and the Entry E baptism reading, the room-for-an-older-son argument against the 1633 Visitation, the separation of the three same-named Francis Gurneys, and the senior West Barsham branch's presence in the East Dereham corridor. The elimination of the other candidates, John's own birth-year window, the trade-admission negatives, the wardship/patronage record, and the case file's probability model stay in their own units.
row.title: Identity — Candidate B: Norfolk parentage

row.scope_summary: The shared matching-criteria profile and elimination scaffold the case file applies across every alternative English John Gurney candidate, and the resulting candidate landscape: three principal alternatives plus the same-name clearance sweep eliminated, five single-attestation households held at a low residual, Candidate B the sole survivor. The case file's own probability model is external-canonical and cross-referenced, not restated. Candidate-specific archival detail lives in the per-candidate units; what the elimination amounts to lives in g13-identity-assessment.
row.title: Identity — candidate overview

row.scope_summary: Candidate D elimination: Robert Gurney of Old Change's son John, admitted to the Drapers' Company by redemption in 1623/4, is documented continuously in London to 1662 -- the same year the colonial John of Braintree died -- eliminating him as the emigrant; the missing wife Mary and matching children give the conclusion a second, independent ground.
row.title: Identity — Candidate D: London Draper, Old Change

row.scope_summary: The 1638 Earsham, Norfolk Gurney yeoman family; the distinct Gurnell surname; a Norfolk household-density survey; a targeted Richard/Isaac negative search; and the wider English probate, parish, and muster comparators that clear the remaining same-name field.
row.title: Identity — Other Eliminations and Earsham

row.scope_summary: The chronology of John Gurney's own age and birth/baptism: the single primary same-person age datum (the 1652/3 Braintree deposition, 'aged 50 or thereabouts'), the c.1602-1610 birth window it fixes, and its reconciliation with the identity work's probable East Dereham baptism (c.1609/10) and the marriage-by-later-1620s bound. The paleographic identification and Candidate-B parentage argument stay external.
row.title: Origin — age and baptism

row.scope_summary: Banks's Bury St Edmunds origin attribution for John Gurney: an unproven 'Banks Mss.' lead, the Newgate-Horningsheath mechanism behind it, the Bury St James/St Mary register searches that clear Bury as the emigrant's birthplace, and the reading that the attribution is consistent with a Norfolk origin. Identity conclusion held to the case file.
row.title: Origin - Bury connections

row.scope_summary: How John Gurney reached and joined the New England community, read from the colonial record: reception into an already-settled Weymouth community rather than a documented shared voyage; no surviving passenger-list or Hingham-corridor record of the crossing; and the reception network as a weak lever for his English origin, which is held to the identity work.
row.title: Origin — migration and reception network

row.scope_summary: The origin/formation bearing of John Gurney's tailoring trade: the two surviving formal trade-transmission pathways (Merchant Taylors' Company; Norwich freemen and enrolled-apprentice registers) both blank for a John Gurney in the emigrant window, the informal/country-training reading that follows, and the de-conflated 1636 Newgate apprenticeship that is the one enrolled 'John Gurney' trade record and is not his.
row.title: Origin — trade and training

row.scope_summary: The American family-memory tradition of a 1615 birth and Southwark origin (explained by conflation with the 1636 Newgate apprentice), the Find a Grave Elm Street Cemetery burial-place lead, and the Gurney colonial-arms tradition weighed against its genuine in-situ Norfolk correspondence.
row.title: Origin — traditions

row.scope_summary: The English wardship-and-patronage network around the senior West Barsham branch in John Gurney's emigration decade: the branch as a Court of Wards minor-heir household (Thomas Gurney III d. vita patris c.1621×1623; his son Edward Gournay a royal ward under his widowed mother Martha Lewkenor after succeeding Henry G15 in 1623, of age c.1628; Edward d. 1641), the 1627 Gurdon–Winthrop letter placing 'mrs. Gurny' inside the Court of Wards circle of Winthrop and Downing, and the Gurdon–Sedley–Lewkenor puritan matrix behind it — assessed as origin-bearing context about the senior branch that neither connects John to it nor traces his crossing, with the identity question held to the case file.
row.title: Origin — wardship and patronage network

row.scope_summary: The standing unresolved questions for John Gurney-1 (English origin and parentage; first wife Mary's identity and English marriage; the untested Y-DNA discriminator), reconciled against the research-leads catalogue; record-location residuals homed in their own topics are cross-referenced, not re-homed.
row.title: Research-state open questions

row.scope_summary: Research-state coverage of the online research infrastructure searched beyond the FamilySearch/Internet Archive/Google corpus - the specialist emigrant compilations, digitized colonial-church indexes, and Massachusetts aggregators - and their uniformly negative returns for John Gurney.
row.title: Research-state source coverage

row.short_label: MBCR 1:331 gunpowder-fine remission (2 June 1641)
row.statement: The Massachusetts General Court order of 2 June 1641 remitted the fine of John Porter, James Ludden, and John Gurney, incurred "for want of gunpowder."

row.short_label: MA Archives gunpowder petition (30 May 1641, 'of Weymouth')
row.statement: The underlying petition, calendared in the Massachusetts State Archives colonial collection and dated 30 May 1641, names "John Gurny, Richard Porter, and James Ludden of Weymouth" seeking remission of the gunpowder fines.

row.short_label: Porter (1878) gloss: 'Ludden and Gurney were of Weymouth'
row.statement: Porter's Genealogy of the Descendants of Richard Porter (1878), p. 225, quotes the 1641 court order and glosses it "Ludden and Gurney were of Weymouth."

row.short_label: Nash (1885): John an original Weymouth grantee before 1643
row.statement: Nash's Historical Sketch of Weymouth (1885), Appendix C, records East Field (p. 258) and Mill Field (p. 278) parcels "first granted to John Gurny/Gurnie" but already held by other men by the 1643 partial property record.

row.short_label: Earliest firm presence: Weymouth by 30 May/2 June 1641
row.statement: John Gurney was living at Weymouth, Massachusetts, by 30 May / 2 June 1641 — his earliest firm New England presence.

row.short_label: Arrival window: 1636–early 1641
row.statement: John Gurney arrived in New England between 1636 and early 1641, most likely in 1638–40. He was absent from the 1636 Weymouth property grants, received ordinary town land there later, and was living at Weymouth by 30 May / 2 June 1641.

row.short_label: Porter forename: petition 'Richard … of Weymouth' vs printed 'John'
row.statement: The petition's image-verified "Richard Porter of Weymouth" reading shifts weight from the printed order's "John Porter," making John Gurney's cleanest 1641 associate a Weymouth/Hull-company comparator rather than a Hingham/Salem Porter.

row.short_label: Braintree residence, c. 1645–1662/3
row.statement: John Gurney lived at Braintree, Massachusetts, from about 1645 until his death in 1662/3 — his settled colonial home after leaving Weymouth.

row.short_label: 1645 Braintree plantation petition (signed)
row.statement: In May 1645 John Gurney signed the inhabitants' petition for the new plantation at Braintree (Mount Wollaston), as reported in the History of Weymouth.

row.short_label: 1652/3 deposition: 'John Gurney of Brayntree'
row.statement: A Suffolk Court Files deposition of 17 March 1652/3 (Wilson v. Faxon) describes "John Gurney of Brayntree aged 50 Yeares or thereabouts."

row.short_label: Tyng farm lease, 1647–1662 (continuous tenancy)
row.statement: In 1647 William Tyng leased John Gurney a 45-acre Braintree farm for ten years; John continued to lease it from Tyng's daughters Bethia and Mercy until 1662, and the same farm is recorded in the 1653 Tyng inventory and the 28 March 1661 estate-division indenture.

row.short_label: Principal Braintree land was the leased Tyng farm (future Adams seat)
row.statement: John Gurney's principal Braintree landholding was leasehold, not freehold: the Tyng farm he held continuously c. 1647–1662 was a tenancy, and the northern part of 'the Gurney farm' later became the Adams family seat (the Old House, Quincy).

row.short_label: 1661/2 Gurney–Thayer deed ('John Gurney, tailor')
row.statement: On 12 February 1661/2 "John Gurney, tailor" conveyed to Richard Thayer, for £14, a Braintree house and orchard, a five-acre Monatiquot-River parcel, and an adjoining half-acre; possession given 16 April 1662, signed by mark, witnessed by Peter Brackett and John Rockwell.

row.short_label: Two distinct Braintree properties: leased Tyng farm vs. Monatiquot freehold
row.statement: John held two distinct Braintree properties in his final years — the leased Tyng farm (the future Adams seat) and his own Monatiquot-River freehold sold to Thayer in 1661/2 — so the 'Gurney farm' of local tradition and his personal homestead are separate parcels.

row.short_label: 1659 Baxter estate: witness and inventory-taker
row.statement: John Gurney witnessed Gregory Baxter's Braintree will in 1659 (with Moses Payne and Richard Brackett) and helped take the estate inventory on 7 July 1659.

row.short_label: Recognised standing in the Braintree community
row.statement: John Gurney held recognised standing in the Braintree community — signing the 1645 plantation petition, serving as probate witness and inventory-taker for Gregory Baxter (1659), and appearing across a dense Braintree creditor network in his own 1663 estate accounts.

row.short_label: Open: pin the 1645 Braintree petition to its primary source
row.statement: Locate the primary page of the May 1645 Braintree (Mount Wollaston) plantation petition naming John Gurney; the current basis is the secondary History of Weymouth report (research lead L-191).

row.short_label: Admitted Weymouth inhabitant (c. 1638/9-1642/4)
row.statement: John Gurney was an admitted, resident inhabitant of Weymouth c. 1638/9-c. 1642/4: early-Massachusetts town land divisions went only to admitted inhabitants, so his three original East/Mill-Field grants mark him as a recognised member of the Weymouth community before his removal to Braintree.

row.short_label: Manuscript Land Grants book: John original grantee of 3 parcels
row.statement: The Weymouth proprietors' manuscript Land Grants book records John Gurney as original grantee of three parcels - two East Field lots (ms pp. 12, 23, under Robert Randoll and Nathaniel Addames) and one Mill Field lot (ms p. 31, under Thomas Richardes), about eight acres in all - each 'first granted/given to John Gurny/Gurnie.'

row.short_label: MBCR 2:79 - 1644 £5 'Mr Ginner' bill (Gurny + Lake)
row.statement: The Massachusetts Bay colony accounts for the General Court session beginning 30 October 1644 record: 'John Gurny his byl for 3. 16. 4d & Tho: Lake his note for 1. 3. 8d are accepted for £5 fro Mr Ginner.'

row.short_label: Credit tie to Rev. Thomas Jenner, Weymouth's minister
row.statement: In 1644, John Gurney and Thomas Lake held claims totaling £5 against Rev. Thomas Jenner, the former Weymouth minister. The record does not say when, where, or why John's claim began.

row.short_label: Weymouth associates: Ludden, Porter, Goodman King
row.statement: John Gurney's documented Weymouth associates were fellow townsmen - his 1641 gunpowder-fine co-petitioners James Ludden and Richard Porter (Porter a 1635 Weymouth settler) and, persisting to his 1663 estate, the creditor 'Goodman King of Waymouth.'

row.short_label: Negative: no active military service
row.statement: No record places John Gurney in active military service: the 1641 powder fine reflects only the ordinary readiness obligation, and a Gurn-variant sweep of the colony military/court records plus a full read of the printed colony records and the Military Company roll (1637-1652) finds him on no campaign, officer, volunteer, or membership list.

row.short_label: Billerica town book - 1659 grant-on-condition & surrender
row.statement: The Billerica manuscript town book records a ten-acre house-lot granted to John Gurney 15 August 1659 'upon condition' he inhabit it himself (his son Richard accepted as a fellow inhabitant), and on 26 December 1659 its surrender: 'Daniel Shead in answer for his father John Gurney; the said John Gurney surrendred up the Lott.'

row.short_label: Hazen Billerica - Dudley-Farm rate & absentee upland share
row.statement: Hazen's History of Billerica records John Gurney assessed 2 pounds 5s 10d toward the half-payment for the Dudley Farm purchase on 10 September 1659, and in the November 1659 upland division 'Peter Bracket and Joseph Tompson holding in common the right of John Gurney, of Braintree' - an absentee share held by other men.

row.short_label: Ballou - John among Braintree men allotted at Mendon, 1662
row.statement: Adin Ballou's History of Milford places John Gurney among the Braintree men accepted to allotments at the new Mendon (Nipmug) plantation in 1662.

row.short_label: SPR #338 - the 1663 'Quinapaug wch we know not' estate line
row.statement: John Gurney's 1663 Braintree probate inventory (taken 16 March 1663; total 55 pounds 14s 6d) records a land-interest line reading 'an estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' - an interest the appraisers could not value.

row.short_label: Suffolk Deeds IV - Quinapaug (Providence-jurisdiction) tract, no Gurney in the recorded deeds
row.statement: Suffolk Deeds Liber IV records the Quinapaug tract: Joshua Foote bought 4,000 acres 'att Quinapaug within ye Jurisdiction of Providence' from the Indians Sacont and George Sacount by deed of 18 June 1655; by 1660 it passed to William Hudson, who sold it in 500-acre parcels to Boston men. No Gurney appears among the recorded Quinapaug parcels.

row.short_label: Finding: Billerica proprietorship (house-lot surrendered; Dudley-Farm share + meadow lots persist); never removed there
row.statement: John Gurney was admitted a proprietor of the new town of Billerica in 1659 - a standing carrying a personal ten-acre house-lot (granted 15 August 1659 on condition he inhabit it, his son Richard accepted as fellow inhabitant), a rate-paying share in the communal Dudley Farm purchase, and two great-meadow lots. He surrendered the house-lot within four months, handed back through his son-in-law Daniel Shed, and never removed to Billerica; the meadow and upland allocations appear in the records independently of the surrendered house-lot, but no Billerica parcel is shown passing to or occupied by a Gurney.

row.short_label: Finding: Quinapaug line = unrecorded Providence-jurisdiction frontier share
row.statement: The 1663 inventory's 'estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' is best read as an unrecorded right or share in the Providence-jurisdiction Quinapaug land speculation (Foote to Hudson to Boston men) - an unvalued frontier proprietary interest, not appraised Braintree real estate.

row.short_label: Analysis: proprietary right, not residence (the 1659-1663 frontier pattern)
row.statement: In 1659-1663 John Gurney repeatedly took up proprietary rights in newly-forming plantations - a Billerica house-lot and Dudley-Farm proprietor's share (1659), a Mendon allotment (1662), and an unlocated Quinapaug frontier interest (by 1663) - and relocated to none of them; the same pattern includes the 1651/2 Weymouth Second-Division great lot granted after he had left that town. The record distinguishes taking up a proprietary right in a new plantation from removing there to live: John's home stayed in the established Weymouth-then-Braintree corridor (his own Monatiquot freehold with house and orchard, sold 1661/2, and the leased Tyng farm he held as tenant). This is proprietary right held separately from residence, not an absence of settlement - John was himself a settler and landholder across several new towns.

row.short_label: Open: Mendon post-1667 record vs John's 1662/3 death (right carried forward vs retrospective)
row.statement: Because Mendon was incorporated only 15 May 1667 and John died 1662/3, his name in the printed Mendon proprietors' record stream postdates his death: it is most plausibly an early 1662 grant carried forward into the later proprietor list or a retrospective allottee entry rather than proof of residence. Whether the 1662 acceptance and the post-incorporation lot are the same right - and how 'John Gurny' and 'Grisel Gurney' as twenty-acre lot-holders relate to the widow/descendants - is developed in the family-Mendon-descendants topic; the manuscript proprietors' images remain the pull.

row.short_label: 1663 probate inventory: itemized movable estate (£55 14s 6d)
row.statement: The manuscript inventory of John Gurney Senr's goods and estate, Braintree, 16 March 1663 (taken by Gregory Belcher, Edmund Quincy, and Thomas Faxon), itemizes his movable estate line by line — apparel, boots and hat; bedding, blanket, pillows and cases; pewter, pincers, brass skillet and kettle; a cupboard and a musket; plough-irons, coulter, axes, mattock and chisel; a chair and frame goods, barrels and trays; wheat and Indian corn with grain-boxes, hoops and tubs; a horse and yoke of oxen; sows, pigs and young cattle; an old barrow, wheels and axletree; and one unvalued land line 'an estate layd out in land at Quinapaug wch we know not' — appraised in all at £55 14s 6d.

row.short_label: Finding: estate wealth concentrated in livestock and the working farm
row.statement: John Gurney's working wealth at death was in husbandry, not his named tailoring trade: livestock alone (horse £9 10s + yoke of oxen £12 10s + swine £6 + young cattle £6) accounted for about £34 of the £55 14s 6d estate, and with plough-gear, cart equipment, and stored wheat and Indian corn the farm economy comes to roughly three-quarters of the whole appraisal.

row.short_label: Finding: a sparse but sufficient household
row.statement: John Gurney's household goods were modest and few — his own apparel, boots and hat (£4 5s) his single most valuable possession, plus bedding (£2 12s), a little pewter and brass (14s 6d), one cupboard (8s), a chair and frame goods, barrels and trays (16s 6d), and an ordinary household musket (12s), with no plate, glass, books, or surplus furniture — a working colonial home furnished to sufficiency and no further.

row.short_label: Negative: no tailoring tools or cloth in the estate
row.statement: The 1663 estate inventory contains no tool or stock of the tailoring trade — no shears, needles, thimble, pressing- or goose-iron, yard-measure, or cloth/fabric — despite John being styled 'John Gurney, tailor' in his 1661/2 Monatiquot conveyance. The absence does not unsay the trade (the deed is direct evidence) but qualifies its centrality to his late-life economy, whose appraised value sat in land-rights and livestock; the 'pincers' listed beside the pewter are a general household/smith's tool, not a tailor's implement.

row.short_label: Analysis: an all-movable estate with no valued real estate
row.statement: The 1663 appraisal is essentially all personalty because John held no valued real estate at death: his principal Braintree farm was the leased Tyng tenancy he never owned, the one freehold he had held outright (the Monatiquot house and orchard) he had sold to Richard Thayer in February 1661/2, and his sole land entry — the Quinapaug interest — was an unpriced frontier share the appraisers 'know not.' The £55 14s 6d therefore measures his movable estate alone.

row.short_label: Record coverage: a continuous 1641-1663 civic/land/court/probate footprint
row.statement: John Gurney's surviving documentary footprint is broad within four record classes — colony court and account records, town land books (Weymouth, Braintree, Billerica, Mendon), a registry deed, a court deposition, and probate (as witness/appraiser and as decedent) — and runs continuously from his earliest secure record (the 2 June 1641 Weymouth gunpowder-fine remission) to his 16 March 1663 estate inventory.

row.short_label: Anderson GMD p.158 - published coverage summary; origin 'Unknown'
row.statement: Anderson's Great Migration Directory (2nd ed., 2025), p. 158, summarizes John Gurney's documented New England presence — arrival 1636, settlements Boston and Braintree — records his English origin as 'Unknown,' and rests the entry on six cited records (Winthrop's Journal 2:422; Massachusetts Bay Records 1:331; NEHGR 62:94; Suffolk Probate Case #338; History of Weymouth 3:251; The American Genealogist 10:70-73); it omits the Weymouth residential phase the manuscript town-land records attest.

row.short_label: Analysis: the 1653 deposition is the only record of John's own person
row.statement: The 1653 Wilson v. Faxon deposition ('John Gurney of Brayntree aged 50 Yeares or thereabouts') is the only surviving record that attests a personal attribute of John Gurney himself; every other record fixes his property, credit, or a civic/probate office rather than his person. A man documented across four record classes over two decades is thus attested as a person, as opposed to as a landholder, creditor, or estate, by a single line in one court file. (The weight of the stated age and its birth inference are worked in the origin/age analysis, not here.)

row.short_label: Negative: no vital or church record fixes John's birth, marriage, death, or burial
row.statement: No New England vital or church record fixes John Gurney's own birth, first marriage (to Mary), death, or burial: within the surviving town vital records, church-admission records, and freeman lists naming John Gurney Sr. (c. 1636-1663), none preserves a baptism, marriage, death, or burial entry for him, and he appears on no church-admission or freeman roll — a silence the full run of the printed Massachusetts Bay colony records confirms at first hand, naming him across all five volumes only twice (the 1641 fine remission and the 1644 bill) and never as an admitted freeman, and that Anderson's full-dress directory review independently reflects. His birth survives only as an inference from the 1653 deposition age and his death only as the terminus his March 1663 inventory implies. Scope limits: the one Braintree line matching his traditional 1661 remarriage and his second wife's 1661 death is printed under 'John Cheny'/'Grizell Kidbee' in the 1886 edition and is a distinct reading/identity question, counted here as neither a surviving nor an absent Gurney vital record; and absence in the reviewed set is not proof no such entry ever existed.

row.short_label: Negative: no record states John's English origin
row.statement: No record of John Gurney in New England states his English origin, parentage, or pre-migration residence; the colony, town, court, and probate records that document his American life are uniformly silent on where he came from, and Anderson's Great Migration Directory, having reviewed that surviving set, records the origin as 'Unknown.' This delimits the coverage of the record, not the identity question itself: the English-origin identification (Banks's Bury St Edmunds lead; the Candidate-B reading making John a son of Francis Gurney the Merchant Taylor) is an open matter pursued in the dedicated origin/identity work and is neither resolved nor advocated here.

row.short_label: Anderson GMD (2025): arrival 1636, Boston/Braintree, origin Unknown
row.statement: Robert Charles Anderson's Great Migration Directory (2nd ed., 2025), p. 158, records John Gurney with an arrival of 1636 and New England residences at Boston and Braintree (Weymouth not listed), while leaving his English origin 'Unknown' — the standing published assessment of John's arrival and settlement.

row.short_label: Absent from Weymouth's 1636 Fresh Pond great-lot roll
row.statement: John Gurney is absent from Weymouth's 1636 Fresh Pond 'great lot' roll of sixteen named householders - evidence he was not yet a Weymouth householder as early as 1636, consistent with an arrival after 1636 rather than with the town's founding cohort.

row.short_label: 1651-52 great lot = proprietary right, not residence (John Read comparator)
row.statement: John Gurney's 1651-52 Weymouth great lot no. 16 was part of a deferred laying-out of 'formerly granted' rights that demonstrably carried absentees and dead men (Samuel Newman and John Allin removed to Rehoboth, Thomas Rider to Boston, William Brandon dead by 1647), so his place on it reflects a surviving proprietary entitlement rather than residence; the closest comparator is John Read, who likewise held Weymouth land, took a Tyng Mount Wollaston farm, removed to Rehoboth, and still drew an 18-acre 1651-52 Fresh Pond great lot.

row.short_label: Grants sat inside an Aylesbury-Vale Bucks neighbour cluster (reception)
row.statement: John Gurney's East and Mill Field neighbours formed a coherent Aylesbury-Vale Buckinghamshire settler cluster - Robert Randall of Wendover, William Brandon of Ashton Clinton, and the Hunt/Humphrey families of Lee, whose Buckinghamshire origins are sworn in a 1688 Weymouth deposition (Massachusetts State Archives 129:16) - so his grants mark him as a newcomer received into an established, regionally-clustered Weymouth neighbourhood. The bearing of this cluster on John's own English origin is developed in the immigration-by-association topic, not here.

row.short_label: Occupation: a tailor by trade, a husbandman by economy
row.statement: John Gurney's trade was tailoring — he is styled 'John Gurney, tailor' in his own 12 February 1661/2 Braintree deed, and Sprague's compiled Braintree genealogy likewise enters him as a tailor — but the working economy of his last years was a husbandman's: his March 1663 estate inventory held no tool of the tailoring trade and its value lay in livestock, plough-gear, and grain. His occupation is best read as a trained trade overtaken in practice by mixed farming: a tailor by name, a husbandman by the measure of his goods.

row.short_label: Negative: no Gurney emigrant in Coldham's English Adventurers & Emigrants 1609-1660
row.statement: Ancestry's database of Coldham's English Adventurers and Emigrants, 1609-1660 (High Court of Admiralty examinations) yields, on a surname-wildcard Gurn* sweep, only two hits - both the Bermuda headland 'Gurnard's Head' - and no Gurney person: no G13 John Gurney emigration record appears in this compilation.

row.short_label: Negative: no Gurney transportee in Emigrants in Bondage 1614-1775 within the emigrant window
row.statement: Coldham's Emigrants in Bondage, 1614-1775 on Ancestry records four Gurn-variant transportees, the earliest Mary Gurney (Middlesex, 1683); none falls in the 1614-1665 window, so the G13 emigrant was not a bonded or transported man under any variant.

row.short_label: Negative: no window-era Gurney in Christ's Hospital child-apprentice emigrants
row.statement: Coldham's Child Apprentices in America from Christ's Hospital, London, 1617-1778 on Ancestry yields four Gurn-variant hits on a wildcard sweep, all eighteenth-century; none is a John and none falls in the emigrant window.

row.short_label: Negative: New England's Hidden Histories holds no pre-1690 church record for John's towns
row.statement: New England's Hidden Histories (Congregational Library) holds no pre-1690 church material for John Gurney's towns - Braintree First begins 1697, Boston First 1690, Dorchester First 1727, with no Weymouth or Mendon book - so this specialist colonial-church index adds no record of him.

row.short_label: Negative: Digital Commonwealth returns zero 'Gurney Braintree'
row.statement: The Massachusetts statewide aggregator Digital Commonwealth returns zero items for 'Gurney Braintree'; the largest single portal to digitized Massachusetts collections surfaces no John Gurney material.

row.short_label: Coverage: the online research-infrastructure beyond the core corpus adds no John Gurney record
row.statement: Beyond the FamilySearch, Internet Archive, and Google corpus already worked, the specialist online research infrastructure returns no John Gurney and no Gurn-variant in the emigrant or early-settlement window: Coldham's three Ancestry emigrant compilations (Admiralty adventurers, bonded emigrants, Christ's Hospital apprentices), the Congregational Library's colonial-church index, and the Massachusetts Digital Commonwealth aggregator are each negative or out of window. This bounds the 'immigrant of unknown origin' state to the present reach of the online infrastructure; the one compilation of its class not yet reached is Coldham's Complete Book of Emigrants, 1607-1660 (absent from Ancestry), which with TNA E 157/20 remains the outstanding emigrant-record residual (lead L-170).

row.short_label: Open question: John's English origin and parentage unidentified
row.statement: John Gurney's English origin, parentage, and reason for emigration remain unidentified. No surviving record states where in England he was born or who his parents were; the American colony, town, court, and probate record set is uniformly silent on his origin, and Anderson's Great Migration Directory records it as 'Unknown.' Every identified same-name English candidate has been eliminated or reduced to low probability, leaving a leading working identification and a residual distribution rather than a proof. The candidate disambiguation is the dedicated identity/origin work and is neither resolved nor advocated here; this item records the standing question, not an answer.

row.short_label: Open question: first wife Mary's identity and English marriage
row.statement: The identity of John Gurney's first wife Mary — her maiden name and the place and date of their English marriage — is unrecovered. The 'Richards' surname carried in derivative online trees is unverified. The marriage is bounded to England before 1628 (their daughter Mary married Daniel Shed at Braintree in 1647, so was born by 1631), yet no John Gurney x Mary marriage is indexed in eastern-England collections 1620-1635 outside the eliminated Eythorne, Kent event; the absence best reads as a parish-register coverage gap rather than an out-of-England or absent marriage. A Peter among Mary's kin would explain the otherwise-anomalous naming of John's son Peter.

row.short_label: Open question: untested Y-DNA discriminator (R1b-DF19)
row.statement: A direct-paternal-line Y-DNA discriminator that could test deep Gurney paternity independent of record survival is defined but untested. The FamilyTreeDNA Gurney project's Braintree Big Y-700 tester (kit 576097) sits at terminal SNP R-FTD83678 within R1b-M269 > P312 > DF19 > R-Z27053, a small continental-leaning north-west-European branch — compatible with but far too sparse and deep (pre-surname) to prove a Norman/continental deep origin. The discriminating comparison — whether a documented English-line Gurney shares the DF19 / R-Z27053 branch (the project's other R-M269 tester, kit 365744, and beyond it a recruit-and-test of a documented English line) — is unrun.

row.short_label: Analysis: the open program reconciled to the leads catalogue
row.statement: The open research program for John Gurney reduces to a small set of standing questions — his English origin and parentage, his first wife Mary's identity and English marriage, and the untested Y-DNA discriminator — after the colonial record was worked to exhaustion at the printed and indexed level. The concrete record-location residuals are already homed in their own topics: the emigrant-record residual (Coldham's Complete Book of Emigrants and TNA E 157/20) in g13-research-source-coverage, the primary page behind the May 1645 Braintree petition, and the post-death Mendon proprietary stream. The operational record-pulls that would test these questions are maintained in the research-leads catalogue, which is the canonical de-duplicated index; this research-state topic surfaces only the work-in-progress subset not yet assimilated into the library, grouped by the question it serves.

row.short_label: 1886 Braintree print: 'John Cheny' marriage & wife-death lines, 1661
row.statement: The 1886 printed Braintree town record (Bates ed.) enters John Gurney's second marriage and his first wife's death under a Cheny surname: p. 717, 'John Cheny Senior and Grizell Kidbee,' 9th month 12, 1661 (12 November 1661); and p. 638, 'Cheny the wife of John Cheny,' 7th month 20, 1661 (20 September 1661). Both dates match the Gurney chronology but the printed surname is Cheny, not Gurney.

row.short_label: Braintree manuscript: fair-copy ink reads 'John Girny'; 'Cheny' is a later pencil margin note
row.statement: The Braintree town-record manuscript, read at image level, shows the fair-copy marriages register (p. 174) ink main text as 'John Girny, Senior (and) Grizell ——X——, by Peter Brackett, 9mo 12, 1661' — the groom 'Girny,' an attested Gurney variant, carrying the copyist's uncertain-reading underline; the bride's surname left blank. 'Cheny / Kidbee' appears only in a later pencil hand in the left margin. The 17th-century original deaths page reads '[?]eny the wiffe of John [?]eny dyed the 7th month 20, 1661,' the initial letterform ambiguous between secretary-hand Ch and G.

row.short_label: Pope 1900: printed Braintree 'John Cheny' a typographical error for John Gurney
row.statement: Charles Henry Pope, The Pioneers of Massachusetts (1900), entering John Gurney of Braintree under the head-form 'GURNET, GORNET,' states that 'he is called John Cheny, Sen., in the printed records of Braintree, by a typographical error,' and reads both the 20 (7) 1661 wife-death line and the 12 (9) 1661 marriage to 'Grizzell, widow of Henry Kibbee' as the Gurney family — an independent, records-based 1900 ruling that the printed Cheny is an error for Gurney.

row.short_label: 'John Cheny' of the 1661 Braintree record = John Gurney
row.statement: The 'John Cheny' of the 1661 Braintree marriage and wife-death lines is John Gurney. The fair-copy manuscript reads 'John Girny, Senior' in ink, with 'Cheny' only a later pencil margin annotation that the 1886 print mistook for text; Pope 1900 independently ruled the printed Cheny a typographical error; no John Cheney family is otherwise attested at Braintree in 1661; and the surrounding facts fit Gurney — Mary Gurney's death three weeks earlier, the officiant Peter Brackett (a documented Gurney associate), and John Gurney's 1663 Braintree probate. Confidence is roughly 85-90%, the residual being the ambiguous deaths-page letterform.

row.short_label: Second marriage: John Gurney m. widow Grizzell, Braintree 12 Nov 1661
row.statement: John Gurney married the widow Grizzell — 'Grissell of the many marriages' — at Braintree on 12 November 1661, by Peter Brackett, as the fourth of her five husbands (Thomas Jewell, Humphrey Griggs, Henry Kibby, John Gurney, and, after John's 1663 death, John Burge in 1667). The marriage is attested directly as John Gurney by Holman's TAG marriage-chain study and by Torrey, independent of the misread town record. Grizzell's compiled maiden name Fletcher (daughter of Robert Fletcher of Chelmsford, Essex) is a colonial attribution and carries no bearing on John Gurney's English origin.

row.short_label: First wife Mary (maiden name unknown), m. England by mid-1620s, d. Braintree 20 Sep 1661
row.statement: John Gurney's first wife bore the name Mary in the compiled Braintree genealogy (Sprague, p. 695); the primary Braintree town record and Torrey both leave her unnamed - the death record enters only 'the wife of John' - and the 'Mary Richards' of later derivative trees is untraced to any primary record. He married her in England by the mid-1620s, bounded by their daughter Mary Gurney's 1647 Braintree marriage to Daniel Shed (baptized Finchingfield, Essex, 1620), which places the daughter's birth by c. 1628. By every indication she was the mother of his children, though no birth record survives to establish the maternity of any of them. She died at Braintree on 20 September 1661.

row.short_label: Negative: no indexed English John Gurney x Mary marriage (wildcard-level)
row.statement: No English record of John and Mary's marriage has been found, despite extended searching of the indexed English parish collections across FamilySearch, Findmypast, Free UK Genealogy, and Ancestry. The search reaches even variant- and misspelling-tolerant wildcard queries: a Findmypast England Marriages sweep for any G*rn* groom marrying a Mary (with spelling variants), 1620-1634, run both with and without the forename John, returns no East Anglian John Gurney x Mary event - the only East Anglian Gurney-surname hit being an unrelated Robert Gvrney x Mary at Norwich, 1622. The absence is best read as a coverage gap in the surviving and indexed parish registers for the couple's home parish rather than as evidence against an English marriage.

row.short_label: Reconstructed family group: five children (Sarah, Mary, Richard, John Jr., Peter) + Isaac uncertain, all Mary's
row.statement: John Gurney's children form a reconstructed family group of five — Sarah, Mary, Richard (the direct-line G12), John Jr., and Peter — with Isaac a probable but unproven sixth; all were born to his first wife Mary, and no single colonial record enumerates the family, which is assembled from compiled genealogies (Sprague, the Weymouth town history, Rigler) and per-child primary records.

row.short_label: Torrey p. 331 cross-check of the John1 family group
row.statement: Torrey's New England Marriages Prior to 1700 (p. 331) gives a one-page cross-check of the John1 Gurney family group, corroborating John's dates (born c. 1603, died 1663) and preserving John Jr.'s Mendon household (wife Ruth; children John, Samuel, Mary).

row.short_label: Isaac (c. 1643) most plausibly John-1's son, by elimination (moderate)
row.statement: The young Isacke Gurney of the 1663/4–1667 colonial court records is most plausibly John Gurney-1's son: no record states his parentage, but an Isaac born c. 1643 needs a father of John's generation, and the only other regional Gurney male, Richard (G12, b. c. 1630–34), was himself a child in 1643 — a moderate identification the dedicated subject file still holds cautiously as a distinct person.

row.short_label: Isacke Gurney court cluster: Scituate 1663/4; Suffolk file 792, 1667
row.statement: A young Isacke Gurney appears in a tight cluster of colonial court records — whipped for pilfering at Scituate (Plymouth court, 1 March 1663/4) and jailed for vagrancy and burglary at Medford, committed to the Boston prison under Daniel Gookin's warrant (Suffolk County court file no. 792, June 1667); neither record states his parentage.

row.short_label: 1652/3 'aged 50' deposition
row.statement: In a Suffolk County deposition in Wilson v. Faxon, entered under Suffolk Court Files no. 188 and dated 17 (1st month) 1652/3 — 17 March 1652/3 old style — 'John Gurney of Brayntree' declared himself 'aged 50 Yeares or thereabouts'. It is his only surviving first-person statement of his own age.

row.short_label: Born c.1602-1610 (probably c.1603-08)
row.statement: John Gurney was born about 1602-1610, most probably about 1604-1608. Three independent estimators of his birth year - his 1652/3 deposition age, the identity work's probable East Dereham baptism (a 'John son of ffrancis Gurnie' about 1609/10), and the bound set by his daughter Mary's 1647 marriage - overlap around 1604-1608, the most probable window, and widen to about 1602-1610 at their possible extremes. A fourth handle, the September 1611 marriage of his probable parents, sits in tension with the baptism reading rather than adding a vote. No colonial record states his birth or age beyond the deposition, and his baptism is not independently fixed apart from the contested Norfolk register reading.

row.short_label: Reconciling the deposition age and the baptism reading
row.statement: The birth-year evidence resolves into a probable window and a wider possible one rather than a single year, and the four handles are not equally strong. The deposition age is the primary same-person datum but a rounded one: 'aged 50 or thereabouts' in 1652/3 centres on 1602/3 yet, once decade-rounding is allowed for, spans a probable 1603-1608 and a possible 1598-1610. The East Dereham baptism is a stronger kind of record but reads several years younger, about 1609/10, with a +/-2-year margin whose early edge (about 1607) closes much of the gap. The bound from daughter Mary's 1647 marriage requires John to have been an adult by about 1625, consistent with the earlier end. The parents' September 1611 marriage is the softest handle: a child can be born before a formal marriage, and on the identity reading a John baptised about 1609/10 would predate it - a strain on the East Dereham picture more than a fifth vote. The three birth-year estimators overlap around 1604-1608; none fixes a year, and John's own baptism stays unproven on independent evidence.

row.short_label: No Merchant Taylors' binding or patrimony freedom for John
row.statement: The Merchant Taylors' Company of London apprentice and freedom records for 1583-1800 (Scott's full transcription of the binding books and freedom registers, UKDA-SN-9263) contain no binding of a John Gurney son of Francis Gurney to any Merchant Taylor master and no Gurney freedom by patrimony at all: the two John Gurney apprentices in the dataset are a glover's son of 'Moborne', Worcestershire (bound 1602) and an Aylesbury ironmonger's son (bound 1655), neither the emigrant, and the 3,391-record patrimony sheet returns zero Gurney variants. The colonial John's tailoring was therefore not transmitted through his proposed father's own livery company, whether by apprenticeship to a fellow Merchant Taylor or by patrimony freedom after Francis Gurney's death.

row.short_label: No John Gurney in the Norwich freemen or apprentice registers
row.statement: The Norwich city freemen register (Millican, 1548-1713) and the enrolled Norwich apprentice-indenture index (Rising & Millican, NRS 29) record no John Gurney freedom admission and no enrolled apprenticeship in the colonial-emigrant window, c.1615-1660. The registers' Gurney content is otherwise Elizabethan (a John Gurney freed not by apprenticeship in 1560/61; a John Gurney cordwainer dead by 1580) plus a single seventeenth-century entry - James Gurney, son of Francis of St Peter Parmentergate, bound at Michaelmas 1627 for seven years and admitted freeman under Henry Bond in January 1648 - which is a Norwich-side record of a Francis Gurney household, not the emigrant. The East Anglian formal trade-transmission pathway thus carries no record of John's training.

row.short_label: John's tailoring learned off the enrolled books (informal/country training)
row.statement: Both surviving formal trade-transmission pathways being blank, John Gurney's tailoring was most plausibly acquired by informal or country training that generated no enrolled indenture or livery freedom - an artisan formation consistent with an East Anglian market-town or country craft upbringing but leaving his specific master, place, and route of training unrecorded. The reading narrows rather than proves: many competent tradesmen never enrolled an indenture or took up a company freedom, so the negatives bound the record of his training, not the fact that he was trained; his trade remains one of the sharpest un-exploited handles on his English origin.

row.short_label: The 1636 Newgate 'John Gurney' apprentice is not the Braintree emigrant
row.statement: The 21 July 1636 Newgate apprenticeship names a different John Gurney, not the Braintree emigrant. The apprentice was apparently born about September 1615; the Braintree John reported himself about fifty in 1652/3, pointing to c. 1602/3, and had married by the mid-1620s with a daughter born by c. 1628. A man born c. 1615 would have been about nine to thirteen during that family period. This is a chronological incompatibility, not a claim that an early end to the apprentice's term constrained the emigrant's arrival.

row.short_label: Reception into an established Weymouth community, not a shared voyage
row.statement: John Gurney's migration reads as the reception of a newcomer into an already-established Weymouth community rather than arrival with a known emigration party: the men he is first grouped with in the 1641 gunpowder-fines record — James Ludden (an Old Planter by 1632) and Richard Porter (a 1635 Hull-company settler) — and his later Weymouth creditor John King were all settlers of a half-generation's standing, not fellow newcomers.

row.short_label: No Gurney on the near-window Boston-area passenger lists
row.statement: No John Gurney — or any Gurney/Gourney/Gurny variant — appears on the three surviving named passenger/settler lists nearest John's 1641 Weymouth appearance (the Bevis 1638, the Diligent of Ipswich 1638, and the Mary Anne of Yarmouth 1637, as transcribed by Drake and arranged by Banks), and no named Boston-area manifest survives at all for the 1639–mid-1641 window; John's ship and Atlantic crossing are undocumented.

row.short_label: No Gurney in the Hingham reception-corridor records
row.statement: A full-text search of the early Hingham, Massachusetts town records — the adjacent community whose Norfolk emigrant cohort makes it the one testable reception corridor — returns no Gurney of any variant, and the fullest untested Hingham source, the Rev. Peter Hobart journal, remains unread; no surviving record places a transient Gurney at Hingham between 1638 and 1641.

row.short_label: Reception network is a weak lever for English origin
row.statement: The reception network fixes the mode of John's settlement but not his English origin: his documented colonial associates and landlords span Buckinghamshire, the West Country, Essex, Warwickshire, Suffolk, and Norfolk with no single stream claiming him, so association is strong enough to show he entered an existing community yet too diffuse to name the corridor that carried him — the English-origin corridor question is therefore held to the identity work, not resolved from the migration record.

row.short_label: 1627 Gurdon–Winthrop letter: 'mrs. Gurny' presents through the Court of Wards
row.statement: Brampton Gurdon of Assington's letter to John Winthrop, 20 October 1627, asks Winthrop — then an attorney at the Court of Wards and Liveries — to further a clergyman's suit to the Master of the Wards over a church presentation held by 'mrs. Gurny who is gardyon to her sonn who wantethe a few monthes of being of ful age,' whom 'yong mr. gurney' attends, with commendations to Emmanuel Downing. It is the only Gurney-variant document in the whole Winthrop Family Papers.

row.short_label: West Barsham wardship: Edward Gournay a minor ward to c.1628 (WARD 7 / C 142)
row.statement: The West Barsham heir was a royal ward through the later 1620s. Thomas Gurney III (Henry G15's eldest son, m. Martha Lewkenor of Denham) died in his father's lifetime, c.1621×1623 — Henry G15's will of 1 May 1621 still names 'my eldest sonne Thomas' among the living — and Henry himself died in 1623, so his grandson and heir Edward Gournay (b. 1608) succeeded as a minor: a ward of the Crown under his widowed mother Martha, coming of age about 1628. Edward held West Barsham to his death on 6 August 1641 (inquisition C 142/613/60). Earlier 'Gurney, Thomas: Norfolk' entries in the Court of Wards series (WARD 7/57/157, /80, 1616/17–1617/18) cannot be Thomas III's death inquisitions — he was living in 1621 — and are carried only as unresolved catalogue leads.

row.short_label: Muskett: the Gurdon–Sedley–Lewkenor puritan matrix (no Gurney in the volume)
row.statement: Muskett's Suffolk Manorial Families grounds the English network behind the 1627 letter: Brampton Gurdon married Muriel, a Sedley-of-Morley and Knyvett-of-Ashwelthorpe granddaughter, and the 1591 will of Martha Heigham of Denham names Martha Lewkenor (the future Mrs. Gurney) among the Denham Lewkenor daughters and endows an Emmanuel College scholarship — the Denham puritan-gentry matrix. No early-modern Gurney appears anywhere in the volume; the Gurdon–Gurney link runs solely through the Sedley/Lewkenor channel.

row.short_label: The senior West Barsham branch inside the founders' Court-of-Wards network, 1623–1641
row.statement: In John Gurney's emigration decade the senior West Barsham branch of the Gurney family stood inside the personal network of the Massachusetts Bay founding leadership: after Thomas Gurney III died in his father's lifetime (c.1621×1623), his son Edward Gournay succeeded Henry G15 in 1623 as a minor ward, and Edward's widowed mother worked — through the leading Suffolk puritan patron Brampton Gurdon — to John Winthrop and Emmanuel Downing at the Court of Wards, out of a Sedley/Lewkenor matrix rooted at Emmanuel College. This is a new English-side record class contemporaneous with the emigration; it makes a Norfolk Gurney's arrival in Winthrop's colony network-consistent, without itself supplying the arrival.

row.short_label: A weak lever for John's origin; the connection is held to the identity work
row.statement: For John Gurney's own origin the wardship-and-patronage network is a weak lever: it establishes that the senior West Barsham branch stood within the founders' circle but does not connect John to that branch, name him in these records, or trace a crossing through the Winthrop channel — 'yong mr. gurney' is Edward the heir, not John. Whether John belongs to that family, and whether he emigrated inside its network rather than in the West-Country Weymouth stream he is actually found among, is the identity question, held to the John Gurney identity case file and the origin candidate files.

row.short_label: Open: identity of 'mr. Warford' and the advowson (CCEd unexhausted)
row.statement: The clergyman 'mr. Warford' whom Mrs. Gurney presented in 1627 is unidentified: no Warford of any spelling appears in Venn's Alumni Cantabrigienses (to 1751), and none in Foster's Oxford register beyond too-early Bristol men. The Norwich diocesan institution registers (the Clergy of the Church of England Database) are the remaining route, and his institution would name the Gurney-held advowson.

row.short_label: Parents' marriage: Francis Gurney x Margaret Rybett, 1611
row.statement: Francis Gurney — the Norwich-and-London Merchant Taylor who is the probable father of John Gurney-1 in the identity work — married his first wife Margaret Rybett at St Martin at Palace, Norwich, on 23 September 1611 ('Franc Gurny & Margaret Rybett'). On the identity reading of John as this couple's eldest child, the marriage is a fourth chronological handle on John's birth window, and a point of friction: it sits later than the probable East Dereham baptism of about 1609/10, which would put John's birth a year or two before his parents married. The marriage record is not in doubt; the parentage identification behind its bearing is probable, not proven, and is held to the identity work.

row.short_label: The deposition age is decade-rounded (age heaping)
row.statement: John's deposition age is a rounded self-report, not a birth date. Early-modern English deponents characteristically gave their ages to the nearest five or ten - the documented 'age heaping' preference for round numbers - and the Wilson v. Faxon file would be expected to show the same round-age pattern among its several deponents, though that file is an unpulled lead not examined here. Read strictly, 'aged 50 or thereabouts' in 1652/3 yields a birth about 1602/3; allowing for the rounding, John's true age could plausibly run from the middle forties to the middle fifties, so the deposition's probable birth range is about 1603-1608 and its possible range about 1598-1610. The datum shows John was an older rather than a younger man but does not fix a birth year.

row.short_label: John's trade points back to a Norfolk textile family
row.statement: John's tailoring is an origin-bearing handle that points back toward a Norfolk textile family. He is styled a tailor in his own Braintree records, and in this period a craft passed most often from father to son. The father the identity work proposes for him, Francis Gurney, was himself a Merchant Taylor - apprenticed in London in 1599, free of the Company in 1606 - whose commercial life ran through Norwich and who in 1622 joined a scheme to teach the poor of King's Lynn to spin worsted-yarn, alongside a Great Ellingham woolchapman; the wider Gurney family sat in East Anglia's worsted-and-woollen economy for generations. So the trade sets a specific expectation - a tailor's son of a tailoring family should be traceable to a master - and strengthens, without proving, the association with Norfolk, the Gurney family, and Francis in particular. The parentage conclusion is held to the identity work.

row.short_label: Passenger silence is expected in the 1639-41 Great-Migration tail
row.statement: The absence of a passenger record for John's crossing is what Great-Migration timing predicts. His arrival is bounded to 1638-early 1641, the tail of a migration that crested in 1638 and fell off sharply after 1640; and named Boston-area passenger lists survive far worse for 1639-mid-1641 - the window most likely to hold his crossing - than for the earlier peak years, the surviving evidence there being ship-arrival notices and clearance licences with passenger counts but no names. A man arriving then would very often leave no listed name even under perfect record-keeping, so his absence from the surviving lists is the expected outcome of poor list survival, not evidence about his party or origin.

row.short_label: The Weymouth land-and-neighbour reception network
row.statement: John's first colonial ground was a Weymouth land-and-neighbourhood network, not a party he arrived with. His East and Mill Field parcels - town grants taken up as an admitted inhabitant in his arrival years and largely passed on by the 1643 property record - sat among neighbours drawn from Weymouth's two documented settler streams, an Aylesbury-Vale Buckinghamshire group and a West-Country/Dorchester group, several granted their own land in the same few years. The associate rings widen from the men named with him in 1641 through the neighbours who held or absorbed his parcels to his later Braintree probate circle, but none resolves into a shared shipload. Read as immigration by association, the evidence shows a newcomer entering an existing community by land, locality, and acquaintance.

row.short_label: The Norfolk-Hingham reception corridor fits a Norfolk origin
row.statement: Adjacent Hingham is the reception corridor that fits a Norfolk origin. New England towns drew regionally concentrated cohorts, and Hingham's was overwhelmingly Norfolk - Daniel Cushing's list gives 206 who came from Norfolk and settled there 1633-1639, the 1638 Diligent alone bringing about 133 - out of Hingham, Wymondham, Attleborough, Great Ellingham, and the Dereham neighbourhood, the very parishes framing the Gurney Norfolk world, including Great Ellingham (Henry Gurney G15's seat), Hingham (the family's Gurney's Manor), and East Dereham (John's probable baptism parish). Weymouth itself was West-Country-led with a Buckinghamshire stream and no Norfolk feed, so a Norfolk John would be an outsider to Weymouth's founders but a natural fit for the Norfolk colony under ten miles away, across the town line his lots abut. A Norfolk arrival received through Hingham is thus the one reception model that suits the favoured origin; the origin case itself is held to the identity work.

row.short_label: Banks (1937) p.151 attributes John Gurney to Bury St Edmunds on 'Banks Mss.' alone
row.statement: Charles Edward Banks's Topographical Dictionary of 2885 English Emigrants to New England, 1620-1650 (ed. Brownell, 1937), p. 151, enters 'GURNEY, John | Bury St. Edmunds | [no ship] | Braintree, Massachusetts | Banks Mss.' - attributing the Braintree emigrant's English origin to Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, on the authority of Banks's unpublished working notes alone, with no ship, register, will, or indenture cited. The same page sets him amid a genuine Bury St Edmunds emigrant cohort (Newgate, Clement Chaplin, William Knapp, John Goodrich, Henry Bright, William Townsend, Theodore Atkinson, Peyton Cooke, Samuel Wright), most of them documented from primary records.

row.short_label: Newgate, master of the 1636 'John Gurney' apprentice, was of Horningsheath by Bury St Edmunds
row.statement: John Newgate - the Boston feltmaker who in July 1636 brought a runaway apprentice named John Gurney before the governor - was himself of Horningsheath (Horringer), Suffolk, about three miles south-west of Bury St Edmunds, and lived at Hessett and Bury St Edmunds (then Southwark) before emigrating to Boston in 1633. An apprentice he carried was therefore most plausibly a young man from Newgate's own Suffolk neighbourhood around Bury.

row.short_label: Bury St James registers: only Gurney household is Thomas x Lidda Broddish (m. c.1633-35), too late
row.statement: A Gurney-variant sweep of the Bury St Edmunds St James parish registers (FamilySearch full-text image group DGS 007413310, 1561-1800) finds no John Gurney household capable of fathering the emigrant. The only Bury Gurney family is Thomas Gurney x Lidda (Lydia) Broddish, married about 1633-35 - far too late - whose children were Juda (bap. c.1633/4), a John 'son to Thomas' registered c.1653/4 after the register reopened, and a Thomas (c.1661/2); a separate John Gurney x Elizabeth baptized a William in 1665. Earlier Bury Gurneys are unconnected fragments (William Gurney's daughter Bridgett, 1588; a Mary Gurny in a 1620-24 communicant list).

row.short_label: Bury St Mary burials 1653-56: a Bury 'John Gurney' buried 1653, not the Braintree emigrant
row.statement: The Findmypast National Burial Index records three Gurney burials at St Mary, Bury St Edmunds, in a four-year window - John Gurney buried 11 December 1653, an unnamed Gurney 6 April 1655, and an unnamed Gurney noted 'Wife' 13 May 1656 - read as one continuing Bury Gurney household whose male head, John, was buried in 1653. That John cannot be the Braintree emigrant, who was alive in Massachusetts and died there in 1662/3.

row.short_label: Bury St Edmunds cleared as the emigrant's birthplace - no natal Gurney household in its registers
row.statement: No John Gurney natal household capable of fathering the Braintree emigrant (born about 1602-1612) survives in the Bury St Edmunds parish registers. Across both Bury parishes searched - St James (a full Gurney-variant register sweep) and St Mary (National Burial Index) - the Gurney presence is either post-dated (the Thomas x Lidda Broddish household married about 1633-35) or an unconnected fragment, and the one Bury 'John Gurney' of the period was buried there in 1653. Bury St Edmunds is therefore cleared as the emigrant's birthplace: whatever Banks recorded, it was not a Bury natal record.

row.short_label: Banks's Bury attribution is an unproven lead that most plausibly tracked Newgate's apprentice; consistent with a Norfolk origin
row.statement: Banks's 'Bury St Edmunds' is an unproven lead, not a birthplace - and it is consistent with the favoured Norfolk (Candidate B) origin rather than evidence against it. Sourced only to 'Banks Mss.', with no supporting Bury natal record found, the attribution is best explained by the 1636 apprentice John Gurney whom the Bury-area feltmaker John Newgate brought before the Boston court: that younger man, de-conflated from the Braintree emigrant in the identity work, carried the Bury/Suffolk association, and Banks's memo most plausibly tracked him. Anderson's Great Migration Directory (p. 158) independently declines Banks, entering the origin as 'Unknown'. A Norwich-born son of Francis Gurney who trained at or near Bury would fit Banks's note without contradiction.

row.short_label: American tradition: John Gurney born 29 Sept 1615, Southwark/"Brent" origin
row.statement: Three American genealogical sources give John Gurney a birth of 29 September 1615 in England: American Biography (1926), locating him "probably from Southwark, near London Bridge"; the Lysander Franklin Gurney sketch (1912, an earlier printing of the same tradition, framing John as John Newgate's apprentice); and a Find a Grave memorial (no. 252975617), locating the birth in the anachronistic modern place name "London Borough of Brent, Greater London" (Brent was created in 1965 and cannot describe a seventeenth-century parish). All three repeat the identical date across compilations a century apart.

row.short_label: Find a Grave burial-place lead: Elm Street Cemetery, Braintree
row.statement: The Find a Grave memorial for John Gurney (no. 252975617) places his burial at Elm Street Cemetery, Braintree, Norfolk County, Massachusetts — a specific burial ground not previously named in this file, the identity case file, or any other source consulted. Braintree's own burial ground and town vital records have not yet been searched specifically for a Gurney stone or plot there, so the attribution stands as a citation-worthy lead rather than a confirmed fact.

row.short_label: The 1615/Southwark tradition belongs to Newgate's apprentice, not the emigrant
row.statement: The 1615-birth/Southwark tradition is best explained as the true biography of the 1636 Newgate apprentice, misattached to the older Braintree emigrant. Read backward, the 1636 court order's "serve until age 24, three years from the following 29 September" implies a birth of 29 September 1615 — exactly the date all three American traditions carry — and Newgate himself lived at Southwark before his 1633 emigration, supplying the "near London Bridge"/"Brent" detail as neatly as the birth date. That apprentice is not the Braintree emigrant, who was deposed "aged about 50" in 1652/3 (implying birth c.1602/3, a decade earlier) and whom Newgate's own later will and estate papers do not name. American family memory most plausibly preserved the apprentice's real biography — his birth year, his London-area origin, his tie to Newgate — and attached it to the wrong, older John Gurney.

row.short_label: American arms tradition, corroborated in situ at Norfolk (inheritance unverified)
row.statement: A separate American family tradition holds that the American Gurneys retained arms connecting them to the Norfolk Gurneys: American Biography (1926) states "the Gurney arms kept by the American Gurneys show connection with Norfolk (England) Gurneys," and the Lysander Franklin Gurney sketch (1912) likewise reports arms cherished within the American branch. The claimed blazon, argent, a cross engrailed gules, is independently and contemporaneously attested in Norfolk itself: carved on the West Barsham chancel brass of Edward Gournay (d. 1641) and recorded again among the Harpley church shields, per an 1871 published account of the Gournay heraldry and an independent 1887 parish-by-parish Norfolk survey. The claimed blazon is therefore genuine to the Norfolk Gournays; only the American line's claimed inheritance of it is unverified.

row.short_label: No early American arms witness found (open web search)
row.statement: No early American physical or manuscript witness to the claimed Gurney arms use — bookplate, ex libris, Bible plate, seal, gravestone, or family paper — has been located for the Braintree/Weymouth line. A variant web sweep (Gurney/Gurnee/Gourney/Gurny, paired with those object terms) surfaced only the same 1926 American Biography derivative account. The absence does not settle the question: a genuine early object could sit in a private family collection, historical society, or local museum outside the reach of an open web search.

row.short_label: Family/compiler memory about John Gurney misattaches real facts, rather than inventing them
row.statement: Family and compiler memory about John Gurney tends to preserve real information misattached to the wrong subject, rather than fabricate claims outright. The birth-date and Southwark-origin tradition is the true biography of a different, younger man (the 1636 Newgate apprentice) attached to the older Braintree settler; the arms tradition rests on a genuinely Norfolk blazon whose American inheritance is unverified rather than disproven; and Charles Banks's own "Bury St Edmunds" attribution for John is a parallel case, a twentieth-century compiler's note that likewise proved to track the Newgate apprentice rather than either proving or disproving a Norfolk origin. Read together, the pattern is a caution for weighing any further tradition that surfaces about him: expect real information pointing at the wrong target before expecting invention.

row.short_label: Shared matching-criteria profile: tailor, wife Mary, five named children, birth c.1602–1610, gone from England by 1641
row.statement: Any English candidate for the Braintree emigrant must satisfy one shared profile drawn from his colonial baseline: a tailor by trade; married to a wife named Mary who bore children Sarah, Mary, Richard, John, and Peter; born in England within a c.1602–1610 window read off his own 1652/3 age deposition; and gone from the English record by the time he first appears in Massachusetts in June 1641. A settled Puritan household is a soft fifth criterion. This whole profile, not a bare surname match, is the shared test applied to every alternative candidate.

row.short_label: The elimination scaffold: structural grounds, not a blanket same-surname suspicion
row.statement: Against the matching-criteria profile, a household is eliminated on structural rather than circumstantial grounds: continuing documented English residence past June 1641; a wife whose name is not Mary; a child set that does not match or that collides in date; or a documented trade, death, or generation placing the household in the wrong period. A household attested by only a single indexed event with no continuing record is held at a low residual (1–3%) rather than eliminated outright, since one record cannot itself rule out an unrecorded emigration. This is the same family-status-and-chronology standard already applied once inside this graph, where it separates the Braintree emigrant from the 1636 Newgate apprentice.

row.short_label: Candidate landscape: 45 eliminated, 5 unlikely, Candidate B the sole survivor; probability model external-canonical
row.statement: Applying the shared matching-criteria profile and elimination scaffold across the full record sweep reduces the field to one surviving named candidate. Of 51 documented same-name English John Gurney households surfaced by the sweeps, three principal alternatives (Candidates A, C, and D) and 45 further households in the same-name clearance sweep are eliminated on structural grounds, and five single-attestation households are held at a low residual rather than eliminated outright. The 1636 Newgate apprentice, already de-conflated from the Braintree emigrant elsewhere in this graph on family-status and chronology grounds, carries no weight in the distribution. Candidate B is the only candidate the profile does not eliminate. The household-by-household enumeration of the cleared field is published in the identity case file at §8 and §8.6, cross-referenced as the master list rather than replicated here; the case file's own probability assessment for Candidate B, including its residual unknown-corridor estimate, is its own argument-specific synthesis and is likewise held external-canonical.

row.short_label: Candidate A: Stewkley baptism, 1628 Bierton marriage, and the 1638-1653 Aylesbury family group
row.statement: A continuous chain of FamilySearch and Findmypast index records places a John Gurney, baptized 21 February 1603 at Stewkley (son of John Gurney), marrying Alice Oliffe at Bierton with Broughton on 24 April 1628, and fathering five children baptized at Saint Mary, Aylesbury, between 16 December 1638 and 12 November 1653 (John, Sarah, Daniell, Jonathan, and Hannah). A separate FamilySearch entry records a further John Gurney marrying Anne Cowheard at the same parish on 25 October 1638; the FS index does not carry a mother's name on the children's baptisms, leaving open whether the 1639-1653 children belong to Alice Oliffe's marriage or a second one, but either reading keeps the household in Buckinghamshire throughout.

row.short_label: At least five distinct Buckinghamshire John Gurney households, 1621-1664
row.statement: A walk of the Findmypast Buckinghamshire marriage, burial, and baptism indexes finds at least five distinct seventeenth-century John Gurney households beyond Candidate A's own: John Gurney + Elizabeth at East Claydon (children Elinor 1632, Samuel 1636; burial 17 Apr 1654); John Gurney + Elizabeth at Chesham (children Andtr, Martha; burials Jul 1672 and 11 Jun 1678); John Gurney + Anne at Wing (children James 1650, Elizabeth 1652); John Gurney + Mary at Cublington (son Isaac, baptized 1664, after the colonial John's own 1662/3 death); and a Luke Gurney household at Aylesbury (four children 1621-1635, not a John Gurney line). A seventh Aylesbury head of household, Edward Gurny, is separately documented (a son buried 1665, a daughter baptized 1666).

row.short_label: 1661 Edlesborough marriage of a John Gurney to Mary Kidgell
row.statement: Phillimore's printed Edlesborough marriage register carries a John Gurney marrying Mary Kidgell in 1661, inside a cluster of five Gurney marriages there between 1660 and 1685 (William Gurney x Martha Halsey 1660; Samuel Gurney of Bierton x Elizabeth Bunce of Padbury 1662; Thomas Gurney of Hockliffe x Frances Norman 1680; George Hill x Mary Gurney 1685).

row.short_label: Candidate A eliminated: continuous Buckinghamshire/Northamptonshire residence, 1603-1653
row.statement: Candidate A's own chain -- the 1603 Stewkley baptism, the 1628 Bierton marriage to Alice Oliffe, the 1638-1653 Aylesbury family group, a 1641 government certificate of residence recording his move into Northamptonshire, and a 1650 Walgrave, Northamptonshire tenancy -- places one continuously documented Englishman in Buckinghamshire and Northamptonshire across exactly the years the Massachusetts John Gurney was building a life at Weymouth and Braintree, dying there in 1662/3. The 1661 Edlesborough John Gurney x Mary Kidgell marriage reinforces the same conclusion from a second angle: either it is Candidate A himself, eliminating him outright on his own English marriage seven weeks after the Braintree John buried his own first wife Mary and remarried, or it is a distinct Bucks household that simply accounts for one more English 'John + Mary' who is not the emigrant. The wider Bucks household map shows the county was in no way short of Gurneys named John, so the surname match carries little weight on its own. Candidate A is eliminated as the colonial emigrant.

row.short_label: 1636 Ackworth marriage of John Gurnoe to Mary Burton; 1637 baptism of John Thomas Gurnoe
row.statement: John Gurnoe married Mary Burton at Ackworth, Yorkshire, on 6 June 1636. A son, John Thomas Gurnoe, was baptized at the same parish on 19 January 1637, seven months later; the baptism transcript does not index a mother's name. No burial of either spouse and no further child are indexed for this household in the present Findmypast coverage.

row.short_label: Ackworth held at a residual ~3%: the only wife-name match, capped by naming and corridor mismatches
row.statement: The Ackworth household is the only same-name comparator in the record sweeps whose wife is genuinely named Mary in roughly the right window, which keeps it visible rather than clearing it outright. Two structural problems weigh against it being the emigrant: the first child is John Thomas, born seven months after the marriage, not Sarah (the colonial John's first child, born about 1628); and Yorkshire sits outside the Norfolk-Suffolk-Essex-London corridor that produced the Great Migration, with no primary record bridging an Ackworth Gurnoe household to any Massachusetts arrival or to the colonial John's known associates. Weighing the other way, the colonial John's own English marriage to Mary is independently bounded to before 1628 by his daughter Mary's chronology, so the 1636 Ackworth bride can only be a hypothetical second English marriage, and the household's disappearance from the indexed Yorkshire record after 1637 has the shape of an unrecorded emigration. Older compiled Gurney genealogies giving the colonial John's wife as 'Mary Barton' or 'Mary Burton' also make this the first primary record to supply that exact name at a plausible date.

row.short_label: Open: parish-register image pull, burial search, and the Mary Barton/Burton tradition-provenance test
row.statement: Three lines of work could move the Ackworth estimate in either direction: a West Yorkshire Archives or Borthwick Institute image pull of the 1636-1637 Ackworth register, to recover the 1637 baptism's parents and confirm the marriage spelling and any further children; an Ackworth burial-register search for either spouse (not yet indexed by Findmypast); and tracing the earliest compiled-genealogy occurrence of the 'Mary Barton/Burton' tradition. If that tradition predates the availability of modern indexes, it is independent evidence pointing at Ackworth and the estimate should rise; if it first appears only after IGI-era derivative trees became available, it is circular and the estimate should hold.

row.short_label: 1638 Earsham will: testator, wife Mary, son John a minor at fourteen, brother Syon/Lyon
row.statement: John Gurney of Earsham ('Eursham'), Norfolk, yeoman, made his will on 10 August 1638, sick in body, holding messuages, lands, and tenements at Earsham both freehold and copyhold. His wife, Mary, was to hold the estate during their son's minority, then take a 4-pound annual annuity in lieu of dower.
